cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
A convex mirror looks simple, but finding its focal length needs a clever
setup.
With a real object in front of it, the image is virtual, behind the mirror.
We cannot catch that ordinary image on a screen.
Instead, a convex lens helps us send in converging rays.
Place an object pin beyond the lens's focal distance.
Align the pin tip, lens centre and mirror pole on a horizontal optical bench.
The lens alone would make a real image at a point we will call C.
Put the convex mirror between the lens and that point, reflecting side facing
the lens.
Adjust the mirror until returning light passes back through the lens and forms
an inverted image at the object pin.
Move your eye sideways and remove relative motion between the two pin tips.
That is the parallax check, not simply overlap from one viewpoint.
Why does this reveal the radius?
A ray aimed at the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror meets the surface
along its normal.
It reflects back along the same path.
At the return condition, the lens's would be image C is that centre of
curvature, behind the mirror.
The distance from the mirror pole P to C is its radius R.
In the paraxial spherical mirror model, focal length magnitude is half that
radius.
Now remove the mirror without moving the lens or object pin.
Locate the lens's real image C with an image pin, again removing parallax.
The pole to image separation gives the radius.
Use supervised safe illumination, never sunlight or direct beam viewing.
A small aperture and careful alignment help keep this spherical mirror
approximation reliable.
Let's turn that ray story into a calculation.
Suppose the mirror pole is at forty centimetres on a scale increasing toward
the original lens image.
After removing the mirror, the real image C is at seventy centimetres.
Their observed separation is thirty centimetres.
It is not the lens to image distance, and it is not yet the focal length.
Calibration shows that the true pole to pin separation is zero point two
centimetres larger than this upright difference.
The corrected radius is thirty point two centimetres.
Divide by two to get focal length magnitude fifteen point one centimetres.
Take a moment: why add the correction before dividing?
Because it belongs to the measured separation.
Adding the full correction to fifteen would give the wrong answer.
With the original incident direction toward the mirror taken positive, the
centre and focus lie behind the convex mirror, so its Cartesian focal length
is
positive.
Here is an uncertainty check.
Each position reading has maximum uncertainty zero point one centimetres.
The index correction has maximum uncertainty zero point zero four centimetres.
For a worst case difference, add their absolute uncertainties: zero point two
four centimetres in radius.
Halving gives zero point one two centimetres in focal length.
With matching precision, report fifteen point one zero plus or minus zero
point
one two centimetres under this stated uncertainty model.
These are original teaching numbers, not measurements we performed.
Repeat the return and parallax procedure for several object positions.
The inferred focal length should agree within uncertainty.
Changing the assisting lens does not change the mirror itself.
That final physical check is just as important as the arithmetic.
